title: Use of AI in Mental Health Care: Community and Mental Health Professionals Survey
type_of_paper: Cross-sectional web-based survey study with descriptive statistics and thematic analysis
population: Australia-based community members aged 16+ (final sample reported as 107/108 in different sections) and mental health professionals (n=86). Community sample mean age 36.9 years; majority had previous mental health diagnosis or significant difficulties (76/108, 70.4%) and many had seen a health professional for mental health concerns (74/108, 68.5%). MHP sample mean age 41.7 years; professions included clinical psychologists, generalist psychologists, mental health nurses, social workers, psychiatrists/registrars, occupational therapists, counselors/therapists, peer workers, and others.
ai_type_application: General/commercial AI tools, especially ChatGPT, used for mental health and professional support. Community members used AI for quick advice when emotionally distressed, as a personal therapist/coach, mood tracking, therapeutic chatbots, personalized recommendations, early detection/monitoring, and crisis intervention support. Mental health professionals used AI for research/literature analysis, report and letter writing, administrative assistance, training/simulation, assessment/diagnosis support, personalized treatment recommendations, tracking client progress, and enhancing client engagement.
mental_health_outcome: Self-reported perceived benefits, harms, concerns, and attitudes regarding AI use for mental health and emotional well-being support; not clinical symptom change. Community members also reported K10 psychological distress at baseline (mean 22.8, SD 8.9), but no pre-post intervention outcome was measured.
positive_effects: Among community members who used AI in the previous 6 months, 77% (23/30) reported AI was very beneficial, somewhat beneficial, or beneficial. Main perceived benefits: availability/accessibility (20/30, 67%), low cost compared with therapy (18/30, 60%), privacy (16/30, 53%). Community free-text themes: improved accessibility and efficiency, excitement about technological advancement, potential for personalized care. Among mental health professionals who used AI, 92% (34/37) reported AI was beneficial. Main perceived benefits: helpfulness (25/37, 68%) and time saving (25/37, 68%). MHP free-text themes: increased efficiency, improved accessibility of care, and possible better diagnostics/treatment support.
negative_effects: Among community AI users, 47% (14/30) experienced harms/concerns. Reported concerns included outputs being too general or not personalized (11/30, 37%), uncertainty about where data was going/privacy issues (11/30, 37%), lack of human connection, possible errors/misdiagnosis, and not picking up serious distress signals. Among MHP AI users, 51% (19/37) experienced harms/concerns. Reported concerns included outputs being too general (12/37, 32%), inaccurate (10/37, 27%), uncertainty about ethics of professional use (9/37, 24%), overreliance by clinicians, regulatory challenges, and data governance/security concerns. The paper also cites an example outside the survey where the Tessa chatbot provided weight-loss advice contrary to eating-disorder guidelines.
evidence_type: Observational self-report survey evidence on current AI use and perceived effects; thematic analysis of open-ended responses
main_finding: Commercial AI tools are already being used by both community members and mental health professionals in mental health contexts. Around 28% of community members and 43% of mental health professionals reported AI use in the previous 6 months, most commonly ChatGPT. Most users perceived benefits, but nearly half also reported harms or concerns. The study concludes that AI may improve accessibility, cost, personalization, and efficiency, but integration into mental health care should be cautious due to concerns about human connection, ethics, privacy, regulation, inaccuracy, misuse, and data security.
limitations_bias: Online recruitment via social media may have attracted more technology-familiar respondents. Small sample size and snowball sampling limit representativeness and generalizability. Inconsistent reported CM sample size (107 vs 108). Benefits and harms may be underestimated because effects may be hidden or delayed. Study measures perceptions and experiences rather than objective mental health outcomes or causal effects.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as indirect evidence on perceived effects of AI on mental health support and mental health care delivery, especially benefits and harms of general AI/chatbot use. However, it does not test efficacy on clinical mental health outcomes, so it is more useful for contextual evidence on acceptability, usage patterns, and reported risks than for estimating treatment effects.
notes_for_research_question: Include if the review captures broader AI effects on mental health support, perceived benefits/harms, or real-world use of AI in mental health care. Exclude from meta-analysis of clinical effectiveness because there is no intervention-control comparison and no pre-post mental health outcome attributable to AI. Useful for discussion of implementation, safety, ethics, and real-world consumer/professional experiences.
